newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania says new Moldova leader will boost ties.
newsitem.headline: Romania says new Moldova leader will boost ties.

text.p: Romania congratulated Petru Lucinschi on his victory in Moldova's presidential election on Monday and said he would boost ties between the two culturally close neighbours.

Petre Roman, chairman of the Senate and number two in the state hierarchy, said Lucinschi's pledges to pursue market reforms "will ensure the healthy development of the economy and stronger relations between the two Romanian states".

Roman, who served as Romania's first post-communist prime minister, said closer ties with Europe, and Romania in particular, "represent the long-term solution for solving the numerous and difficult problems faced by Moldova's people".
About 60 percent of Moldova's 4.3 million people are ethnic Romanians who share a common culture and history.

Most of the former Soviet republic was formed of territory taken from Romania by the Kremlin under the 1939 Nazi-Soviet pact. Talk of reunification, widespread after the collapse of the Soviet Union, has all but died away in both countries.

Romanian politicians watched the Moldovan election with considerable interest, but ties with ethnic kin next door have paled in importance to a campaign to win admission to NATO and the European Union.

Lucinschi, a former top communist and chairman of the national parliament, was widely viewed as more favourable to Moscow than defeated incumbent Mircea Snegur. In his campaign, he reminded voters that Russia was an important neighbour which supplied most of Moldova's energy.

Calls for the recreation of "Greater Romania" incorporating territory now part of ex-Soviet Moldova and Ukraine and Bulgaria are confined to one party which won five percent of the vote in last month's general election.
On Sunday, Romania's national day, private ProTV broadcast interviews from people on both sides of the border with Moldova saying they viewed themselves as part of the same nation.
